nodes.description: For the intraneural form. Resection aims to remove the tumour, with or without a nerve graft. In a 2021 systematic review, in which 40 of 64 surgically managed cases were resected with or without repair, no lesion recurred after resection (the abstract gives no follow-up after resection). The other sources restrict it. A 30-patient series, in which four patients were completely resected and grafted, advises against complete resection to preserve the nerve's residual function and judges the results of grafting poor, suggesting residual tumour cells as one reason. The longitudinal series warns of further iatrogenic deficit with grafting, as in one of its own patients; it says resection with grafting may be considered for focal, more distal lesions without long-term muscle atrophy when the intra-operative nerve action potential is absent or low, but most of its own cases would not qualify, so it advises that resection should usually not be performed. It found no tumour spreading to initially uninvolved nerves on surveillance MRI, though it recognises that longer follow-up is needed. A 2024 review of childhood cases notes that resection is widely held, though without consensus, to be restricted to shorter lesions; it suggests that complete removal may prevent proximal progression where a terminal branch of a single major nerve is involved over a short length, but advises caution for tumours involving major nerves, and it restates an earlier finding that the tumours only rarely grew in length and did not grow to involve new nerves; a 2026 series, in which the one patient resected and grafted (who had an early severe deficit and also a tendon transfer) illustrates the high morbidity, reserves surgery for select cases, particularly short-segment involvement and rapid progression. Outcomes after resection are mixed. In the 2024 review, of ten patients followed up after grafting, five improved mildly (involved segments of 1.5 to 5 cm) and five, recorded as stable, did not (2.5 to 18 cm, one unknown). Of its nine patients excised without a graft, two were followed up: one without motor improvement and one, asymptomatic before surgery, free of recurrence at 6 years. In the longitudinal series, five patients had resection with grafting: the two who were interviewed, both of whom also had tendon transfers, felt the surgery had improved them (one of them is also one of the review's improved patients), while another's wrist and finger extension worsened after a radial nerve resection and grafting, improving gradually but not to baseline when follow-up ended at 6 months.
